input:
With these figures established, attention can now be turned to the wall thickness of the absorber, which is a value that several of the subsequent design decisions will ultimately rest upon. Once the corrosion allowance has been added, the absorber wall thickness comes to 21 mm, and it is this figure, rather than the pressure-only thickness, that will govern the quantity of material to be ordered. It should be noted that the corrosion allowance does not contribute to the strength of the wall in any structural sense; rather, it represents a sacrificial provision, put in place in anticipation of the gradual loss of metal that will occur over the operating life of the absorber, so that the wall which remains at the end of that life is still sufficient for the duty imposed upon it. The 21 mm figure therefore embodies an assumption about the corrosiveness of the service, and it follows that any change in that assumption would feed directly through into the thickness itself.

The gasket selection, by way of contrast, has been approached from a considerably narrower standpoint. The two candidate gasket materials have been compared on the basis of temperature limit only, and on this basis the higher-rated of the two materials emerges as the preferred option. It is important to appreciate, however, what such a preference actually amounts to: it is, in essence, a ranking of ratings rather than a demonstration of performance under service conditions. A temperature limit indicates the boundary up to which a material is rated to operate, but it says nothing about how that material behaves as the boundary is approached. Nor does it take any account of the environment in which the gasket will actually function, an environment characterised in part by the $\Delta P$ developed across the absorber and by the suction conditions, expressed in terms of NPSH, that are encountered at the lean solvent pump. Neither of these considerations is touched upon by a comparison that has been conducted purely in terms of temperature limit, and the extent to which the preferred material will perform satisfactorily in practice therefore remains, at this stage, an open question, pending the point at which the actual service temperature at the joint is brought into the comparison alongside the rating itself.
target:
The wall thickness of the absorber is 21 mm after the corrosion allowance is added. The allowance is sacrificial metal: it is there to be corroded away over the life of the absorber, and the wall remaining at the end of that life is the wall the pressure duty is checked against. The 21 mm figure thus rests on the corrosion assumption behind the allowance, and a change to that assumption changes the thickness by the same amount, with no further calculation in the chain to catch the error.

The gasket comparison is narrower in scope. Two gasket materials are compared on temperature limit only, and the higher-rated material is preferred. A temperature limit is a rating boundary: it states the temperature the material is certified to withstand. It states nothing about the material's behaviour below that boundary, and nothing about the duty the gasket will see in service, where the $\Delta P$ across the absorber and the NPSH at the lean solvent pump are set by the process and not by the gasket. The comparison also omits the service temperature at the joint itself, and it leaves the gasket's other duties untouched: the material must seal at the joint and stay sealed as conditions at the joint change, and a comparison made on temperature limit alone cannot rank the two materials on either count, since neither was examined. The margin between the rating and the temperature the gasket will actually reach is the quantity on which the preference depends, and that margin is not stated anywhere in the comparison. As it stands, the preference for the higher-rated material is a preference between two ratings, formed before the condition that would test the rating has been fixed, and the argument remains open at the point where that condition has to enter it.
